analysis.one_liner: Permanently bars new oil, gas, and mining development on federal land surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park in New Mexico.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently protect the land around Chaco Culture National Historical Park from new oil and gas leasing died in the Senate Energy Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently withdrawn the federal land around Chaco Culture National Historical Park — a UNESCO World Heritage Site in New Mexico that Pueblo tribes, the Navajo Nation, and the Hopi Tribe consider sacred — from oil and gas leasing, mining, and sale. It would have terminated existing oil and gas leases on which no drilling had started, and let the Interior Department transfer the land to an Indian tribe. The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal communities — the Navajo Nation, Pueblo tribes, and the Hopi Tribe — that live near and use the Greater Chaco landscape ceremonially, plus the National Park's visitors, would gain permanent protection from new oil and gas drilling around the park. Residents of the region, who the bill's own findings say have borne health, safety, and quality-of-life harms from extensive natural gas development, would see new drilling blocked on the withdrawn land.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribal communities near Chaco Canyon and park visitors

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently withdraws federal land around Chaco Culture National Historical Park from oil, gas, and mineral leasing, so it could not be sold off, mined, or leased for drilling in the future.
It terminates existing non-producing oil and gas leases on the withdrawn land, stopping leaseholders who hold leases but have never drilled from starting operations later.

It allows the Interior Department to convey or exchange the protected land with an Indian tribe under an approved resource management plan, and it explicitly leaves tribal mineral rights on trust and allotment land untouched.

It protects a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the sacred and cultural sites that Pueblo tribes, the Navajo Nation, and the Hopi Tribe use ceremonially, in an area where extensive natural gas development has affected community health and quality of life.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding non-producing federal leases in the withdrawal area, which would be terminated, and future leaseholders, who would be shut out of new drilling there. Land-managing agencies and adjacent communities that might have counted on energy development revenue would forgo it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas leaseholders and drillers

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal permanently forecloses future oil, gas, and mineral development on the covered federal land in a region where mineral leasing is an economic mainstay, which opponents argue costs New Mexico revenue and drilling jobs and narrows the nation's energy supply.

The bill terminates existing non-producing federal oil and gas leases, ending speculative leaseholders' rights to develop acreage they paid for, even though those leases carry valid existing rights under current law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape and the health of nearby tribal communities at essentially no cost to anyone but a small number of speculative oil and gas leaseholders who have never drilled; the bill exempts active, producing leases, so no one loses a working operation. The design is narrow and even provides carve-outs for utility, water, and road improvements the region needs. The honest objection is that the withdrawal forecloses future energy development on federal land in a state where oil and gas revenue funds schools and services, and mineral owners may view the loss of speculative value as uncompensated. On balance the trade favors the public and tribal communities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2023 and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján, joined by Senator Martin Heinrich, introduced S. 1404 on May 2, 2023.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, the standard first step.
No further action was taken: the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and there was no vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew only one cosponsor in the Senate, leaving it with thin support and no path to a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding non-producing oil and gas leases and any future lessees around Chaco park, who keep the option to drill; the world heritage landscape and nearby tribal communities got no protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas leaseholders around Chaco park

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor; no further action followed.

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in May 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: With Republicans holding the minority in the 118th Senate, no floor time was ever arranged for the bill; as a single-sponsor committee bill it had no mechanism to reach the floor without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record; it had only Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, suggesting a partisan split, but the real blocker was inaction in committee rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill ends future federal oil and gas leasing and mining around Chaco Park and terminates non-producing leases, cutting off drillers' access to acreage in the Mancos/Gallup shale play near the park. For nearby residents, that same activity is the source of drilling-related health and quality-of-life complaints, so the industry's interest ran against the public's here.

industries.industry: Oil and gas royalty owners and leaseholders
industries.note: Companies holding non-producing federal leases around the park would lose those lease rights outright, while producing leases and tribal mineral rights are untouched. The loss is to speculative acreage near a world heritage site, not to operating wells.

industries.industry: Indian tribes (Navajo Nation, Pueblo tribes, Hopi Tribe)
industries.note: The bill lets tribes receive or exchange the protected federal land under a resource management plan, giving communities that claim descent from the Chacoan people a role in managing the landscape they consider sacred. It explicitly preserves tribal mineral rights on their own trust land.
